title: Stacked modality
intro: From C1 on, verbs grow longer rather than newer. This unit stacks forms you already know: a participle such as `-mIş`, `-(I)yor` or `-(y)AcAk`, then a form of *olmak* that carries a modality, a tense or a condition. *Gitmiş olmalı* (she must have left), *gitmiş olacak* (she will have left), *gidecek olsa* (if she were to go), *gitmiş olsaydı* (if she had left). Archaeologists live on such guesses, so many of the examples come from a dig.

sections.title: Gitmiş olmalı: guesses about the past

blocks.text: In [A2 unit 6](gp-meli-inference) you used `-mAlI` for a confident guess about the present: *Evde olmalı* (She must be at home). To guess about the past, put the `-mIş` participle first and *olmalı* after it: *Gitmiş olmalı* (She must have left). The participle never changes; the person ending goes on *olmalı*.

lines: unut- + muş + olmalı + yım → unutmuş olmalıyım

rows.en: he, she or it must have forgotten
you must have forgotten (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **The negative** goes on the main verb, inside the guess: *Mektubu okumamış olmalı* (He must not have read the letter). The participle is then `-mAmIş`.

rows.en: he, she or it must not have forgotten
you must not have forgotten (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **Questions.** A question with *olmalı* sounds odd, because a guess is something you assert. To ask whether something could have happened, use *olabilir mi*: *Yanlış anlamış olabilir miyim?* (Could I have misunderstood?).

rows.en: could he or she have misunderstood
could you have misunderstood (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **May have, can't have.** Swap *olmalı* for the ability forms of [A2 unit 5](gp-abil): `-mIş olabilir` (may have, might have) and `-mIş olamaz` (can't have). Together they make a small scale of confidence about the past.

**In progress.** With `-(I)yor` instead of `-mIş`, the guess is about something going on right now: *Telefonu açmıyor; duş alıyor olmalı* (She isn't answering: she must be in the shower). Plain *Uyumalı* would mean **he should sleep**, so *Uyuyor olmalı* (he must be asleep) removes the doubt.

items.tr: Işıklar yanıyor; çocuklar eve dönmüş olmalı.
items.seg: Işık|lar yan|ıyor; çocuk|lar ev|e dön|müş ol|malı.
items.en: The lights are on: the children must have come home.

items.tr: Anahtarı arabada unutmuş olabilirim.
items.seg: Anahtar|ı araba|da unut|muş ol|abil|ir|im.
items.en: I may have left the key in the car.

items.tr: Bu kadar kısa sürede bitirmiş olamazlar.
items.seg: Bu kadar kısa süre|de bitir|miş ol|a|maz|lar.
items.en: They can't have finished in such a short time.

items.tr: Mesajımı görmemiş olabilir.
items.seg: Mesaj|ım|ı gör|me|miş ol|abil|ir.
items.en: He may not have seen my message.

items.tr: Telefonu açmıyor; duş alıyor olmalı.
items.seg: Telefon|u aç|mı|yor; duş al|ıyor ol|malı.
items.en: She isn't answering the phone: she must be in the shower.

blocks.text: *Gelmeliydi* ([B1 unit 2](gp-should-have)) is **he should have come**, and usually means he didn't. *Gelmiş olmalı* is **he must have come**, a conclusion that he did. The two look alike and say nearly opposite things.

Bare `-mIş` ([B1 unit 3](gp-evidential-mis)) already infers: looking at a wet street, *Yağmur yağmış* (It's rained). *Yağmur yağmış olmalı* adds your reasoning, **it must have rained**, and is the natural choice when you think aloud or argue from clues.
French builds the same guess with devoir: “elle a dû partir” is *gitmiş olmalı*, and “elle doit être chez elle” is *evde olmalı*.

sections.title: Bitirmiş olacağım: will have done, will be doing

blocks.text: To see a future action as already finished, use `-mIş` with *olacak*, the future of *olmak*: *Saat altıda raporu bitirmiş olacağım* (By six I'll have finished the report). Turkish needs no word for **by**: a time phrase, `-DIğIndA` or `-(y)AnA kadar` sets the moment.

lines: bitir- + miş + olacağ + ım → bitirmiş olacağım

rows.en: he, she or it will have finished
you will have finished (plural or polite)
he, she or it won't have finished
you won't have finished (plural or polite)
will he, she or it have finished
will you have finished (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **Will be doing.** With `-(I)yor` instead of `-mIş`, the action is in progress at that future moment: *Yarın bu saatte uçakta uyuyor olacağım* (This time tomorrow I'll be asleep on the plane).

items.tr: Kazı bittiğinde üç evi tamamen kazmış olacağız.
items.seg: Kazı bit|tiğ|i|n|de üç ev|i tamamen kaz|mış ol|acağ|ız.
items.en: When the dig ends, we will have excavated three houses completely.

items.tr: Sen gelene kadar yemeği hazırlamış olacağım.
items.seg: Sen gel|en|e kadar yemeğ|i hazırla|mış ol|acağ|ım.
items.en: By the time you come, I'll have made dinner.

items.tr: Haftaya bu saatte tatile çıkmış olacaklar.
items.seg: Hafta|ya bu saat|te tatil|e çık|mış ol|acak|lar.
items.en: This time next week they'll have gone on holiday.

items.tr: Eylülde raporu hâlâ yazıyor olacağım.
items.seg: Eylül|de rapor|u hâlâ yaz|ıyor ol|acağ|ım.
items.en: In September I'll still be writing the report.

blocks.text: For a guess about now, **they'll have arrived by now**, Turkish prefers *varmış olmalılar* or the `-DIr` of [unit 2](gp-dir-assumption): *Şimdiye kadar varmışlardır*.

Customer-service language has spread `-(I)yor olacak` to plain promises: *Sizi arıyor olacağız* (We'll be calling you). Many speakers hear it as a calque of English and prefer the simple future, *Sizi arayacağız*. Keep `-(I)yor olacak` for an action in progress at a future moment.

sections.title: Gidecek olsam: if it came to that

blocks.text: [B2 unit 10](gp-digi-takdirde) gave `-(y)AcAk olursa`, **if it should happen that**. With *olsa*, the unreal conditional of *olmak*, the case becomes merely imagined or unlikely, and the main clause usually takes the aorist or `-(I)rdI`: *Bir gün Türkiye'den taşınacak olsam en çok çayı özlerdim* (If I were ever to move away from Turkey, I'd miss the tea most).

lines: taşın- + acak + olsa + m → taşınacak olsam
gel- + me + y + ecek + olsa + k → gelmeyecek olsak

rows.en: if he, she or it were to come
if you were to come (plural or polite)

blocks.title: *gelmemek*: if I weren't going to come…

rows.en: if I weren't going to come
if you weren't going to come
if he, she or it weren't going to come
if we weren't going to come
if you weren't going to come (plural or polite)
if they weren't going to come

blocks.text: There is no question form of the clause: the question goes on the main verb, *Bunu satacak olsan kaça satardın?* (If you were to sell this, how much would you sell it for?).

blocks.caption: Five ways to say **if you come**
head: Clause
Meaning
rows: If you should come, if you ever come…
If you were to come, if it came to your coming…

blocks.text: **The past.** `-(y)AcAk olsaydı` imagines a past intention that never existed: *Gelecek olsaydın bize haber verirdin* (If you'd been going to come, you would have told us).

**Was about to.** The same pair in the plain past, `-(y)AcAk oldu`, means **was about to, made as if to**, and usually didn't: *Bir şey söyleyecek oldu, sonra vazgeçti* (He was about to say something, then changed his mind).

items.tr: Bir gün buradan taşınacak olsam en çok bu manzarayı özlerim.
items.seg: Bir gün bura|dan taşın|acak ol|sa|m en çok bu manzara|y|ı özle|r|im.
items.en: If I were ever to move away from here, I'd miss this view most.

items.tr: Yürüyerek gidecek olsak bile yetişiriz.
items.seg: Yürü|y|erek gid|ecek ol|sa|k bile yetiş|ir|iz.
items.en: Even if it came to walking there, we'd make it in time.

items.tr: Bunu satacak olsan kaça satardın?
items.seg: Bu|nu sat|acak ol|sa|n kaç|a sat|ar|dı|n?
items.en: If you were to sell this, how much would you sell it for?

items.tr: Kapıyı açacak oldu, ama birden durdu.
items.seg: Kapı|y|ı aç|acak ol|du, ama birden dur|du.
items.en: She was about to open the door, but suddenly stopped.

blocks.text: The person ending goes on *olsa*, and the participle never takes one: *gidecek olsam*, never *gideceğim olsa*.

You know the unreal past from [B2 unit 1](gp-unreal-past): *Bilseydim gelirdim* (If I had known, I would have come). Writing and careful speech often say it with `-mIş olsaydı`, which stresses a finished action: *Daha erken başlamış olsaydık mezarı bulurduk* (If we had started earlier, we would have found the grave). The two usually mean the same.

lines: başla- + mış + olsaydı + k → başlamış olsaydık

rows.en: if he, she or it had known
if you had known (plural or polite)
if he, she or it hadn't known
if you hadn't known (plural or polite)

blocks.text: As with `-sAydI`, the if-clause has no question form; the question goes on the main verb: *Bilmiş olsaydın gelir miydin?* (Would you have come if you had known?). For **they**, *olsaydılar* is also heard.

**The main clause** takes `-(I)rdI` or `-(y)AcAktI`, as in B2, or `-mIş olurdu` (would have done), which matches the finished action: *Erken çıkmış olsaydık treni yakalamış olurduk* (If we had left early, we would have caught the train).

**Wishes and regrets.** After *keşke* ([B2 unit 1](gp-keske)): *Keşke ona söylemiş olsaydım* (I wish I had told him). Without the past *-ydI*, `-mIş olsa` looks at a present result: *Şimdiye kadar varmış olsalar ararlardı* (If they had arrived by now, they would have called).

head: Form
Example

rows: careful or written; stresses the finished action

blocks.text: C1 texts, academic ones above all, pile these forms on top of each other. Read them as you read the stacked voices of [B2 unit 7](gp-voice-order): from the root out, one suffix, one meaning.

head: Chain
Root out
Meaning
rows: he may not have been able to come
it must not have been possible to find it
they must have managed to walk
he may not have read it
she may not have seen it
*yap-* do → *-ıl-* passive → *-mış* → *olması gerekir* it is necessary that it be

blocks.text: **May not have: two ways.** The negative can sit on the main verb or on *olmak*, with the same meaning: *Mesajı görmemiş olabilir* and *Mesajı görmüş olmayabilir* both say **she may not have seen the message**. But *Mesajı görmüş olamaz* is **she can't have seen it**.

**Could have, but didn't.** Add the past to *olabilir* and the possibility becomes a missed one: *Kaybolmuş olabilirdik* (We could have got lost, but we didn't), against *Kaybolmuş olabilirler* (They may have got lost: we don't know yet). Compare `-(y)AbilIrdI` in [B1 unit 2](gp-could-have).

**Formal guesses** often turn the chain into a verbal noun ([B1 unit 4](gp-ma-possessive)) before *gerek*, *muhtemel* or *mümkün*: *Taşların uzaktan getirilmiş olması gerekir* (The stones must have been brought from far away), *Kentin bir depremle yıkılmış olması muhtemeldir* (The town was probably destroyed by an earthquake).

items.en: They may not have been able to find the grave.

items.tr: Bu taşlar uzaktan getirilmiş olmalı.
items.seg: Bu taş|lar uzak|tan getir|il|miş ol|malı.
items.en: These stones must have been brought from far away.

items.tr: Mesajı görmüş olmayabilir.
items.seg: Mesaj|ı gör|müş ol|ma|y|abil|ir.

items.tr: Kaybolmuş olabilirdik.
items.seg: Kaybol|muş ol|abil|ir|di|k.
items.en: We could have got lost.

items.tr: Taşların uzaktan getirilmiş olması gerekir.

blocks.text: Endings come last: the person ending and the question particle go on the final word of the chain. *Gelmiş olmalılar*, *Gelmiş olabilir mi?*, never *gelmişler olmalı*.

summary: `-mIş olmalı` is a confident guess about the past: *Gitmiş olmalı* (She must have left). `-mIş olabilir` is **may have**, `-mIş olamaz` **can't have**.
`-(I)yor olmalı` guesses about something in progress: *Uyuyor olmalı* (He must be asleep).
`-mIş olacak` is **will have done** and `-(I)yor olacak` **will be doing**; the person ending goes on *olacak*.
`-(y)AcAk olsa` imagines an unlikely case: *Taşınacak olsam…* (If I were to move…). In the plain past, `-(y)AcAk oldu` is **was about to**.
`-mIş olsaydı` is the unreal past with a finished action, usually the same as `-sAydI`; its main clause can be `-mIş olurdu`.
Read chains from the root out; the person ending and *mI* go on the last word.
*Gelmiş olmalı* (he must have come) is not *gelmeliydi* (he should have come).
